title: THE BEDROOMS OF KINGS, THE SECRETS OF FAMILIES, AND THE SIN INSIDE THE CHURCH
paragraphs: THE BEDROOMS OF KINGS, THE SECRETS OF FAMILIES, AND THE SIN INSIDE THE CHURCH

The Bible exposes what people hide behind closed doors. But 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 reveals something even more powerful: No past is beyond the cleansing power of Jesus Christ when a sinner turns to Him.
There are sins people commit in public.
And there are sins people spend their entire lives trying to keep private.

There are betrayals that destroy marriages, desires that destroy families, abuses of power that destroy innocent lives, and secret relationships that eventually bring entire households to their knees.
Some happen in royal palaces.
Some happen behind the doors of respectable homes.
Some happen in places where people gather every Sunday to worship God.
And sometimes, the people responsible for the deepest wounds are the very people everyone else considers respectable, powerful, religious, or untouchable.
But here is something uncomfortable about the Bible:
It does not protect the reputation of powerful sinners.
It exposes them.
It does not rewrite the failures of its heroes to make them look respectable.
It records their failures.
And it does not pretend that sexual sin is harmless simply because someone involved has a religious title, a respected family name, or a position of influence.
Yet, in the middle of all this uncomfortable truth, Scripture reveals a hope that is even more extraordinary than the darkness it exposes.
Jesus Christ does not merely expose what sin has done. He offers sinners a way to become new.
And that is where our story begins.
Consider King David.
A man described as a man after God's own heart. A warrior. A king. A worshiper. A man who had experienced God's faithfulness in ways most people could hardly imagine.
Yet one evening, from the security of his palace, David saw Bathsheba.
What followed was not simply a moment of temptation.
It became a devastating chain of decisions.

David desired another man's wife. He sent for her. He slept with her. When she became pregnant, he attempted to conceal what had happened. Eventually, he arranged circumstances that resulted in the death of her husband, Uriah.
Read that again.
A king who had conquered enemies could not conquer his own unrestrained desire.
A man entrusted with authority used that authority to take what did not belong to him.
And the tragedy did not end in the bedroom.
It entered a marriage. It cost a man his life. It brought consequences into David's household.
But perhaps the most frightening detail is that David initially continued living as though everything could remain hidden.
Until God sent Nathan the prophet.
Nathan did not flatter the king.
He did not protect David's reputation.
He confronted him with a story that exposed the injustice of his actions.
And then came the unforgettable words:
"Thou art the man." — 2 Samuel 12:7 (KJV)
Imagine that moment.
The palace. The throne. The authority. The reputation.
All of it suddenly confronted by the truth.
David could command an army, but he could not command the truth to disappear.
He could silence people, but he could not silence the voice of God.
And when David finally acknowledged his sin, he cried out in Psalm 51.
One of the most important expressions in that prayer is found in the Hebrew word:
חָנֵּנִי (ḥonnēnî)
Meaning: "Be gracious to me" or "Have mercy upon me."
David was not negotiating with God.
He was not presenting his accomplishments as payment for his failures.
He was pleading for mercy.
In Psalm 51:10, he prayed:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." — KJV
The Hebrew expression for "create" is בָּרָא (bārāʾ), the same verb used in Genesis 1:1 to describe God's creating work.
David was asking for something deeper than reputation management.
He needed God to do an inward work that he could not accomplish through public appearances.
He did not merely need a better public image.
He needed a clean heart.
And perhaps someone reading this understands that feeling.
You can clean your house while your heart remains troubled.
You can smile in photographs while carrying guilt that nobody knows about.
You can attend church, sing worship songs, quote Scripture, and still know that something inside your life desperately needs to be surrendered to God.
But David's story is not permission to repeat his behavior.
His repentance did not erase the consequences suffered by others.
And forgiveness must never be used to silence victims, excuse abuse, or protect powerful people from accountability.
God's grace does not make injustice acceptable.
In fact, the Bible makes another uncomfortable revelation about sexual sin:
Sometimes the people who suffer most are not the people who committed it.
Look at Tamar.
She was a daughter of King David.
Her own half-brother Amnon became obsessed with her and ultimately sexually assaulted her.
The account in 2 Samuel 13 is devastating.
Tamar pleaded with him not to do it. She recognized the wickedness of what he was attempting. She tried to stop him.
But he refused to listen.
The Scripture records that he overpowered her and violated her.
And afterward, the same man who had claimed to desire her treated her with hatred and contempt.
Think about that.
Tamar was not the sinner in that encounter.
She was the victim.
And the Bible does not disguise that reality.

Her suffering exposes something that must never be forgotten: sexual violence is not a love story, consent cannot be replaced by desire, and a victim must never be blamed for the actions of an offender.
Her story also exposes the terrible damage that can happen when those with power fail to confront evil properly.
David became angry when he heard what happened, but the account reveals a devastating failure of justice within his household.
And Tamar was left carrying a wound that should never have been inflicted upon her.
This matters because biblical teaching about sexual purity must never become a weapon against those who have been abused.
God does not condemn victims for the sins committed against them.
The responsibility belongs to the perpetrator.
And any church that uses forgiveness language to pressure victims into silence has misunderstood the character of the God it claims to represent.
Grace protects the dignity of the wounded. It does not provide a hiding place for those who wound them.
Now bring this conversation closer.
Not every betrayal happens in a palace.
Some happen in ordinary homes.
A husband secretly entertains another relationship.
A wife discovers messages that shatter her trust.
A family learns that someone they respected has been living a double life.
Children grow up surrounded by the consequences of decisions they never made.
And sometimes, the person who appears spiritually strong in public is fighting a private battle with pornography, adultery, lust, dishonesty, or sexual compromise.
The Bible does not pretend these things are insignificant.
Proverbs 6:32 warns about the destructive foolishness of adultery.
Hebrews 13:4 calls for the marriage bed to be honored.
Ephesians 5:3 instructs believers that sexual immorality and impurity must not characterize their lives.
And Jesus takes the issue even deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He teaches that sexual sin is not merely about what happens physically. He confronts the heart, including the lustful intention that can exist long before an outward act.
Jesus is not interested in superficial righteousness.
He sees beyond the carefully managed appearance.
He sees the heart.
But now comes another uncomfortable question.
What happens when sexual sin enters the church?
What happens when the person who falls is a pastor?
What happens when someone who teaches Scripture is secretly violating the very principles they preach?
What happens when church members discover that a respected spiritual leader has been manipulating people, committing adultery, or abusing the trust placed in them?
Does the title make the sin smaller?
Does the pulpit make the person untouchable?
Does anointing language cancel accountability?
Absolutely not.
The apostle Paul confronted sexual immorality within the Corinthian church itself.
In 1 Corinthians 5, he addressed a shocking case of sexual immorality involving a man and his father's wife.
What made the situation even more disturbing was the congregation's failure to respond with the seriousness the situation demanded.
Paul refused to treat the matter as something insignificant.
He confronted the church because holiness matters.
The Gospel is not a decorative religious accessory that allows people to continue destroying others while maintaining a spiritual reputation.
The church must be a place where sinners can find grace, but it must also be a place where sin is confronted, the vulnerable are protected, and genuine repentance produces change.
Forgiveness does not mean automatically restoring someone to leadership.
Repentance does not eliminate the need for consequences.
And reconciliation does not mean that victims must immediately trust those who have harmed them.
Sometimes accountability includes removal from leadership, legal consequences, safeguarding measures, professional intervention, and a long process of demonstrating genuine change.
These are not enemies of grace.
They can be necessary expressions of truth and justice.
But now, after everything we have uncovered, we must arrive at the Scripture that changes the entire direction of this conversation.
First Corinthians 6:9–11.
Paul begins with a serious warning.
He tells the Corinthians not to deceive themselves about the unrighteous and the Kingdom of God.
He identifies several patterns of sin, including sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse, and exploitation.
Notice something important.
Sexual sin is not the only sin Paul confronts.
The passage is not giving us permission to isolate one category of sinners while pretending that greed, dishonesty, exploitation, and abusive behavior are somehow less serious.
God's holiness confronts the entire human condition.
But then comes verse 11.
And this is where the darkness meets the extraordinary hope of the Gospel.
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." — 1 Corinthians 6:11 (KJV)
Stop for a moment.
Read those words slowly.
"Such were some of you."
Paul was writing to a Christian congregation.
He was reminding them that some of the very people now belonging to Christ had once lived in the sins he had just described.
Their histories were not all clean.
Their backgrounds were not all respectable.
Their pasts were not all suitable for religious photographs.
Some had been sexually immoral.
Some had been adulterers.
Some had been greedy.
Some had been exploitative.
Some had been living in patterns of sin that were completely incompatible with the Kingdom of God.
But something had happened.
They had encountered the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
And Paul does not say, "You were perfect."
He does not say, "You were always respectable."
He does not say, "You never struggled."
He says:
"But ye are washed."
The original Greek word is:
ἀπελούσασθε (apelousasthe).
It comes from the verb apolouō, meaning to wash off or wash away.
Paul is describing cleansing.
Not cosmetic improvement.
Not religious makeup.
Not learning how to hide a scandal more effectively.
Cleansing.
The imagery is powerful because sin leaves a stain that human reputation cannot remove.
You can delete the messages.
You can destroy the evidence.
You can change your social media image.
You can move to another city.
You can convince people that you have changed.
But you cannot cleanse your conscience by managing appearances.
Only God can do the work that the human heart desperately needs.
And the passage continues.
"But ye are sanctified."
The Greek word is:
ἡγιάσθητε (hēgiasthēte).
It comes from hagiazō, meaning to make holy or set apart for God.
This is important.
Jesus does not rescue people merely so they can return to the same destructive patterns.
Grace calls people into a new life.
The person who once treated others as objects must learn to honor their dignity.
The person who once lived in deception must learn to walk in truth.
The person who once exploited trust must learn accountability.
The person who once surrendered to destructive desires must learn to surrender those desires to Christ.
Sanctification is not pretending that temptation disappears overnight.
It is the continuing work of the Holy Spirit, transforming the believer to become more like Jesus.
And then Paul delivers another extraordinary declaration:
"But ye are justified."
The Greek word is:
ἐδικαιώθητε (edikaiōthēte).
It comes from dikaioō, meaning to justify, declare righteous, or pronounce someone to be in the right.
This is the language of God's gracious verdict.
The believer is not accepted because the past never happened.
The believer is accepted because of what Jesus Christ has accomplished.
The cross is not a denial of our guilt.
It is God's provision for our redemption.
And notice how Paul connects these three realities.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
All in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
This is not human self-improvement.
This is the transforming work of God.
And there is something else we must understand about this passage.
Paul is not teaching that people can continue deliberately embracing sin while claiming that grace makes repentance unnecessary.
The entire chapter challenges believers to leave behind the patterns of life that contradict their identity in Christ.
In verses 12–20, Paul continues by explaining that the body belongs to the Lord and that believers must glorify God with their bodies.
He even declares:
"For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's." — 1 Corinthians 6:20 (KJV)
That is the Christian response to grace.
Not, "I can do whatever I want."
But, "Jesus gave Himself for me. How can I continue treating my life as though it does not belong to Him?"
This is where the Gospel becomes deeply personal.
Maybe you are reading this with a history you desperately wish you could erase.
Maybe you betrayed someone who trusted you.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you promised you would never cross.
Maybe pornography has quietly taken control of your thoughts.
Maybe you are trapped in an affair that is destroying more than you realize.
Maybe you have been living two different lives: the person everyone sees on Sunday and the person you become when nobody is watching.
Or perhaps you are the one who was betrayed.
The one who discovered the messages.
The one who was lied to.
The one who was manipulated by someone you trusted.
The one who still struggles to understand how a person could speak about God while doing something so devastating to another human being.
Listen carefully.
If you are the one who sinned, do not use this message to excuse yourself.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin before God.
Turn away from the behavior.
Accept appropriate accountability.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where necessary.
Do not demand immediate trust from the people you have wounded.
Do not confuse being forgiven by God with being entitled to the restoration of every position, relationship, or privilege you previously enjoyed.
And if you are the one who was wounded, do not allow someone else's sin to convince you that you have lost your worth.
You are not responsible for another person's betrayal.
You are not required to pretend that the pain did not happen.
You can seek safety, justice, healing, and wise counsel while still bringing your broken heart before Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not only for the person who needs forgiveness.
It is also good news for the person who desperately needs healing.
Consider the woman in John 8.
She was brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.
The religious leaders wanted to turn her into an instrument of condemnation.
They placed her shame in the middle of a public confrontation.
But Jesus challenged the hypocrisy of those accusing her.
One by one, they left.
And when Jesus spoke to the woman, He did not tell her that sin was irrelevant.
He told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11 (KJV)
There it is.
Grace and transformation.
Mercy and a call to a different life.
Jesus did not humiliate her to demonstrate His holiness.
Neither did He tell her to remain in the life that had brought her there.
He offered mercy and called her forward.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus does not need to pretend your sin is harmless in order to offer you forgiveness.
He went to the cross precisely because sin is so serious and humanity is so desperately in need of redemption.
At Calvary, the innocent Son of God bore the cost of our salvation.
He was crucified, buried, and raised again.
And through Him, forgiveness is offered to everyone who comes to God in genuine repentance and faith.
Romans 5:8 reminds us that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners.
Not when we had perfected our reputation.
Not when we had cleaned up every corner of our history.
Not when we finally became impressive enough to deserve His attention.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
This is why our message must always remain:
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because the wounds were imaginary.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because the final chapter of a surrendered life does not have to be written by its worst moment.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Yet Jesus restored him and entrusted him with responsibility in John 21.
Paul persecuted the church.
Yet Christ transformed him into an apostle who proclaimed the Gospel.
The thief crucified beside Jesus had a past he could not undo.
Yet he turned to Christ in his final hours and received the promise of paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
Different stories.
Different circumstances.
One extraordinary Savior.
And that is the hope we must never stop proclaiming.
Your past may explain some of your wounds, but it does not have to become the master of your future when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Now, perhaps you understand why this message needs to travel beyond the person currently reading it.
Someone you know is hiding a secret.
Someone is struggling with sexual temptation.
Someone is carrying the guilt of adultery.
Someone is recovering from betrayal.
Someone has been hurt by a person who used religion to conceal wrongdoing.
Someone believes that God could never welcome them again.
Someone needs to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and transformation is available through Jesus Christ.
Do not assume someone else will reach them.
Be honest before God.
Your honesty may encourage someone who has been suffering silently.
There may be a day when you need to remember these words, or when someone you love needs to read them.
We want people to encounter the truth of Scripture, the seriousness of sin, the beauty of grace, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, not something we buy or earn (Ephesians 2:8–9).
It is not a replacement for the biblical tithe or offerings you may give through your local church, and it is certainly not a purchase of God's blessing.
It is simply an opportunity to stand behind a ministry whose message you believe should reach further.
There is also something else we want every serious student of Scripture to discover.
These resources are there to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their understanding of biblical truth, develop their prayer lives, and become more intentional in following Jesus.
We want to build more than a social media audience.
We want to help build a community of believers who are serious about growing in Christ.
You do not have to make a financial contribution to help spread the Gospel. Your willingness to share biblical truth can help this message reach someone who needs it.
Because ultimately, this is not about building a name for a ministry.
It is about making the name of Jesus known.
And if there is one thing I want you to remember after reading this entire message, it is this:

The Bible never tells us that sin is harmless. It shows us exactly how devastating sin can become. But it also reveals a Savior whose grace is greater than the shame of a repentant sinner, whose blood is sufficient to cleanse, and whose Spirit can transform a life that once seemed beyond repair.
David needed mercy.
Tamar deserved justice.
The Corinthian church needed correction.
The woman in John 8 needed mercy and a new direction.
And humanity needs Jesus.
So perhaps the most important question is not whether your past contains something shameful.
Perhaps the question is whether you are willing to bring that past into the light of Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply having a past marked by failure.
It is hearing the invitation of Jesus and continuing to choose the darkness.
Never let your scandal become bigger in your eyes than the Savior who went to the cross to redeem you.
And never forget:
The same Gospel that exposes the darkness also announces the possibility of a new beginning.
Jesus still saves.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
And Jesus still rewrites everything.
Because somebody, somewhere, is still waiting to discover that their story does not have to end where their worst mistake began.
The past may have left a scar, but in the hands of Jesus, even a scar can become a testimony of grace.
